answer.label: Not Winston Churchill — an evolved saying, finalized in 1930s ad copy
answer.authorDates: Aphorism attested 1920–1938 · earliest full form in a 1938 Budweiser advertisement
answer.sourceLine: This line appears nowhere in Churchill’s speeches, books, or letters — the International Churchill Society ↗ confirms it is not in his canon. Quote Investigator ↗ traces it from partial sayings in 1920–1921 to a full match in a 1938 Budweiser beer advertisement; the Churchill credit only surfaced in the 1960s. No single originator is documented.

source.excerpt: They found contentment in the thrill of action, knowing that success was never final and failure never fatal. It was courage that counted.
trail: Quote Investigator ↗ reconstructs a multi-year evolution: George Starr White’s 1920 volume (“Success is never final”) and George Matthew Adams’s 1921 essay Finality (“Your success is not final—nor is your failure”) supply fragments; a 1938 Budweiser advertisement is the earliest full match.
The International Churchill Society ↗ and historian Richard Langworth report the line is “found nowhere in his canon” and list it among quotes falsely attributed to Churchill.

The Churchill credit is a 1960s development: coach Joe Paterno attributed it to Churchill in 1968 ↗, repeating it in his 1971 book, and John Wooden did the same in a 1972 memoir — a textbook case of “Churchillian Drift.”
source.excerptNote: The closest documented ancestor of the modern quote: copy from a 1938 Budweiser advertisement, as reproduced by Quote Investigator ↗. Note the wording (“never final…never fatal…courage that counted”) differs from the polished modern version now pinned to Churchill.

source.rightsNote: The exact modern wording cannot be tied to any single, identifiable authored work: its closest documented ancestor is anonymous copy in a 1938 Budweiser advertisement, and the partial 1920–1921 sources use different phrasing. Because the origin of the precise quotation is unknown, no public-domain or copyright status can be responsibly asserted.

author.name: Winston Churchill
author.heading: The name it was pinned on
author.metaLine: 1874–1965 · British Prime Minister, statesman & Nobel laureate in Literature
author.bio: Winston Churchill really did produce a mountain of memorable, quotable prose — which is exactly why unattributed aphorisms drift onto his name. Gnomologist Nigel Rees coined the term “Churchillian Drift” for this: the true author gets elbowed aside and a more famous figure takes the credit. This particular line is a documented casualty — listed among the quotes falsely attributed to Churchill by the International Churchill Society.

misattribution.heading: A textbook misattribution
misattribution.intro: The quote is one of the internet’s most-shared “Churchill” lines — and one of the best-documented fakes.

items.why: Churchill scholars have searched exhaustively and come up empty. The International Churchill Society ↗ states the line is “found nowhere in his canon” and lists it among the quotes falsely attributed to him.
Some online sources pin the saying on Lincoln instead, but none supplies any citation in the Lincoln record — there is no evidence he ever wrote or said it.

misattribution.truthLine: The earliest full-form match is anonymous ad copy in a 1938 Budweiser advertisement; per Quote Investigator ↗, the Churchill credit only appears in the 1960s, long after the words were already circulating.

context.heading: Why it stuck to Churchill
lead: The saying did not spring from a single speech or pen. It condensed, over nearly two decades, out of interchangeable maxims about success, failure, and courage — the kind of uplifting copy that circulated in self-help books, syndicated columns, and, tellingly, beer advertising. By the time it reached its familiar polished form, it read like something a great orator might have said, which is precisely how misattribution works.

In the 1960s, coaches and motivational speakers began invoking “Churchill” as the author, and the credit calcified. This is the mechanism Nigel Rees named “Churchillian Drift” — anonymous wisdom gravitating toward the most quotable famous name available.
context.pull: An anonymous ad slogan, dressed up in a statesman’s reputation.
